doc.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010

title: Standards versus modal tunes: tension and release
summary: Songbook tunes suit improvising because of tension to release; he finds 'So What' harder, a result of Upstate training.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Speaking of the Real Book and the number of tunes in it that date back to the Great American Songbook —
How come? How come those songs that were not really written as jazz tunes per se offer such a rich palette of —

Well because you said it. Because the songs really, you can improvise on them. They’re made perfectly to improvise. You see, I don’t want to get too technical, but to me improvising is about tension to release. You have a tension and you release it, in other words you resolve it. Okay? And even when you don’t resolve it, the tension is, like you said, it’s up in the air, to be resolved. And that’s all right too. And a lot of these American Songbooks have that. They have the tension to the release. And to put it in musical, in theoretical terms, it’s the dominant to the tonic. And these tunes that we were talking about, like they might be in one key but within that form you go to about five keys. What does that mean? You have to have the tension to the release. The tension to the release. Tension to the release. So that’s perfect for a jazzer, they want to deal with it, to improvise. It’s like putting a carrot in front of a rabbit. You know?
Well do you find it harder than, or a different kind of challenge to improvise like on a tune like “So What,” where you’ve just got two chords and they’re just —

Um hum. Exactly. I understand what you mean. Well to me it’s almost sometimes harder. For me. Because I mean just for the fact, well the more I study music the more I realize how many tensions are in there. See? At first I just looked at it as one thing. The Dorian mode let’s say. But no, it’s more than that. You start learning how you could — that’s the foundation. You could learn how you start building upon it. And I’m still working on that. Thinking about that. And then you could relate that to other songs too. See that’s what guys are doing today. They’re taking their modal kind of things and putting it on these standards. And inside the tension to the release. You know what I’m saying? I don’t want to get too technical, but that’s simple I think. That’s just tension to release. So you could add tension to that long 16 bars of D Dorian, and you can look at it a lot of different ways. But at first, to me, all that space made it much harder for me. For me. Not the rest of the world. That came from the Upstate, Tony Leonardi school, and Sal Nistico, © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

change-change-change-change-change-change. And which I loved. But I’m saying but then when I got to “So What” I said what do I do? D Dorian for eighteen thousand years. And then it goes up a half step. But you know, but I mean, but to me they’re both great. But yeah, it does present a challenge, because that’s hard to resolve with all that movement with keys in the Songbook, that’s hard too. Because you’ve got to know your keys. But you’ve got to know your keys when you’re talking about superimposition on the Dorian mode. See? So it’s all the same.
